questions.q: In the fraction 3/4, which number tells us how many equal pieces the whole was divided into?
questions.a: The number 4. If a student answers 3, they have confused the numerator (the part we have) with the denominator (the total number of parts).

questions.q: If you share a chocolate bar equally between 2 friends, each gets 1/2. If you share that same bar equally among 4 friends, each gets 1/4. Which piece is bigger, and why?
questions.a: The 1/2 piece is bigger. A wrong answer (thinking 1/4 is bigger because 4 > 2) reveals the student is looking at the numbers as whole integers rather than understanding that a larger denominator means the same whole is being split into more, smaller pieces.

questions.q: Draw a rectangle and shade 3/5 of it. How many equal parts should you divide the rectangle into?
questions.a: You must divide it into 5 equal parts and shade 3. If the student divides it into a different number, they do not understand that the denominator represents the total number of equal divisions required to define the "whole."

questions.q: If a pizza is cut into 8 equal slices and you eat 2, what fraction of the pizza did you eat? If you then cut those 8 slices into 16 smaller slices, how many of those new smaller slices would represent the same amount of pizza?
questions.a: You ate 2/8 (or 1/4). You would need to eat 4 of the new smaller slices (4/16). A wrong answer suggests the student struggles to see that different fractions can represent the same physical amount (equivalent parts).

questions.q: A friend says, "I have 1/10 of a cake, and you have 1/5 of a cake, so I have more because 10 is bigger than 5." Is this reasoning correct?
questions.a: No, the reasoning is incorrect. 1/5 is larger than 1/10 because if you split a cake into only 5 pieces, each piece is much larger than if you split it into 10 pieces. The student likely ignored the "part of a whole" concept and treated the denominator as a simple counting number.

questions.q: Create a scenario using everyday objects (like pencils or apples) where you would use a fraction. Explain why you used those specific numbers.
questions.a: A good answer would involve a clear "whole" (e.g., a packet of 6 pencils) and a "part" (e.g., taking 2 pencils out). A poor answer fails to ensure the parts are "equal" or misidentifies the total as the numerator.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A fraction ______ a part of a whole, where a "whole" is divided into equal segments.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you have one round roti and you want to share it ______ with a friend.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to visually represent a fraction, identify the numerator and denominator, and explain that a larger denominator means smaller individual pieces when sharing a single whole.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ you have one round roti and you want to share it equally with a friend.
